explanations.answer: He fought the Ammonites without calling them
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Ephraim, one of Israel's tribes, asks Jephthah, “Why have you crossed over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you?” Picture finding out about the party from the photos afterward. Folks get loud when they feel left out, baker.

explanations.answer: He kept the Ammonite land for Gilead
explanations.explanation: I get why that sounds right, because land fights are common. But the text never mentions Jephthah keeping any land. The complaint Ephraim states is about the call that never came: “…without calling us to go with you?” Stick with what the verse says and you'll stay out of trouble.

explanations.answer: He made a treaty with the Ammonites
explanations.explanation: No treaty here, friend. Jephthah, Gilead's leader, fought the Ammonites, and the verse says nothing about a deal with them. Ephraim's complaint is that he went to fight “without calling us to go with you.” A treaty would've been a whole different conversation.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: True. Jephthah says, “My people and I had a serious conflict with the Ammonites, and when I called, you did not save me out of their hands.” So in his telling, the call went out and Ephraim didn't answer. Ephraim says they were never called, and Jephthah says they were. That's two very different versions of one phone call.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Careful, baker, this one flips it. Jephthah says the opposite of what this statement denies: “…when I called, you did not save me out of their hands.” He says he did call, and Ephraim didn't come through. So he answers their complaint by saying he asked first.

explanations.answer: LORD
explanations.explanation: Right. Jephthah says, “…the LORD delivered them into my hand.” He tells Ephraim he risked his life and crossed over, and then he names who gave the win. He doesn't hand the credit to himself. A leader who points up is a good thing to see.

explanations.answer: Gileadites
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since Jephthah's people are Gileadites and he says “My people and I” had the conflict. But when he gets to the win, he names someone else: “…the LORD delivered them into my hand.” The verse puts the credit with the LORD. Jephthah himself says so.

explanations.answer: elders
explanations.explanation: Not elders, friend. In this speech to Ephraim, Jephthah never mentions them. He says, “…the LORD delivered them into my hand.” The LORD is the one he names for the win.

explanations.answer: Why have you come today to fight against me
explanations.explanation: That's his closing question: “Why then have you come today to fight against me?” He's just walked through what happened, and then he turns it back on them. I think he's saying, "After all that, this is what you came for?" That's me guessing, but it sure sounds like it.

explanations.answer: Why did you wait so long to answer my call
explanations.explanation: Close in spirit, but those aren't his words. Jephthah says he called and Ephraim didn't save him, but he never asks about waiting. His last question is about the present: “Why then have you come today to fight against me?” Ephraim is the one standing in front of him with a threat.

explanations.answer: Why should Gilead share its spoils with you
explanations.explanation: Spoils never come up in this passage, baker. Jephthah's last words to Ephraim are a question about why they're there: “Why then have you come today to fight against me?” It's short and it lands. There's no sharing of anything in that speech.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Jephthah gathers all the men of Gilead and fights Ephraim, and the verse says “the men of Gilead struck them down.” Ephraim showed up ready to fight and didn't come out on top. Gilead won this one.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: False is right. The text says Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead, fought Ephraim, and “the men of Gilead struck them down.” Ephraim came with a threat to burn his house down, and it was Ephraim who got struck down. Big talk, baker, doesn't always bring a big win.

explanations.answer: You Gileadites are fugitives in Ephraim
explanations.explanation: Yes. The verse says it was because the Ephraimites had said, “You Gileadites are fugitives in Ephraim, living in the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh.” That's the insult the text points to. Words can start something big, baker, so mind yours.

explanations.answer: You Gileadites are cowards in battle
explanations.explanation: Sounds like a classic insult, but it isn't the one in the verse. Ephraim's words were about where Gilead lived: “You Gileadites are fugitives in Ephraim…” The text doesn't say anything about cowardice here. The quote is the one to hold on to.

explanations.answer: You Gileadites have no real leader
explanations.explanation: Funny thing, Jephthah is the leader standing right there. What the Ephraimites said, according to the verse, was “You Gileadites are fugitives in Ephraim, living in the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh.” Nothing about leaders in it. That insult was about fugitives.

explanations.answer: Ephraimite
explanations.explanation: That's the question at the fords: “Are you an Ephraimite?” The Gileadites have captured the crossings, so anyone who wants over has to answer them first. The question comes when a fugitive from Ephraim says, “Let me cross over.” It's a simple question, and everything hangs on it.

explanations.answer: Ammonite
explanations.explanation: The Ammonites are the people Jephthah just fought, so I see why they came to mind. But the man at the ford is a fugitive from Ephraim, and the Gileadites ask him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” The Ammonites aren't part of this scene. This fight is between Gilead and Ephraim.

explanations.answer: Amalekite
explanations.explanation: Amalekites do show up in this passage, but way down in 12:15, as the hill country where Abdon is buried. They aren't in the scene at the fords. There the Gileadites ask, “Are you an Ephraimite?” Right name, wrong place.

explanations.answer: He could not pronounce it correctly
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The man says “Sibboleth,” “because he could not pronounce it correctly,” and that's how they know him. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the passage, because it ends with men being seized and killed at the fords. It's a hard scene to read.

explanations.answer: He did not know what it meant
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about meaning. What gives him away is that he said “Sibboleth,” “because he could not pronounce it correctly.” It was about how the word came out, not what it meant. This is a heavy scene, so it's worth getting right.

explanations.answer: He answered too slowly at the ford
explanations.explanation: Speed isn't mentioned anywhere in the verse. The Gileadites asked him to say “Shibboleth,” and he said “Sibboleth,” “because he could not pronounce it correctly.” That's what gave him away. I think this part of the story is a heavy one.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not Jephthah, friend. The verse says he was “buried in one of the cities of Gilead.” You're thinking of the last judge in the passage: Abdon was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites (Judges 12:15). Easy to mix up, since the burials come one right after the other.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: False is right. Jephthah judged Israel six years, and when he died, he was buried “in one of the cities of Gilead.” That's his home region, not Ephraim's hill country. The Ephraim burial belongs to Abdon at the end of the passage (Judges 12:15).
